example.problem: You owe $5,000 on a credit card at 18% APR and pay $150 a month. How long until it is gone, and how much interest do you pay?
steps: First month's interest: $5,000 × 0.015 = $75, so $75 of the $150 payment cuts the balance.
Rounded up: 47 months, just under 4 years.

howItWorks: Each month, interest is added to your balance and then your payment is subtracted. The calculator first converts the APR to a monthly rate, then uses the payoff formula months = −ln(1 − r × balance ÷ payment) ÷ ln(1 + r) to find how many payments it takes. It then simulates the balance month by month so the total paid and total interest figures are exact, including the smaller final payment.

These are estimates for planning purposes, not financial advice. Real debts may add fees, penalty rates, or changing APRs, and this assumes you make no new purchases on the account. If debt feels unmanageable, consider speaking to a nonprofit credit counselor.
intro: Find out how long it takes to pay off a credit card or loan balance at your current monthly payment, and how much interest you will pay along the way. Enter the balance, the APR, and what you pay each month.

mistakes.text: If your payment only covers the interest, the balance never shrinks. On $5,000 at 18%, paying $75 a month means you owe $5,000 forever.
mistakes.title: Paying less than the monthly interest

mistakes.text: The APR is yearly. Dividing by 12 gives the monthly rate — using 18 directly instead of 0.015 breaks the formula completely.
mistakes.title: Using the annual rate as the monthly rate

mistakes.text: On the $5,000 example, $200 a month instead of $150 saves about 15 months and roughly $580 in interest. Small increases compound in your favor.
mistakes.title: Not raising the payment when you can

mistakes.text: New purchases add to the balance this formula is paying down. The payoff time assumes the balance only shrinks from here.
mistakes.title: Keeping spending on the same card
